lessons.title: Workbooks, sheets and the grid
learn: Cells, ranges, rows, columns, Name Box, formula bar, status bar
What the status bar tells you about a selection
lessons.mac:
Right-click = Control-click, or a two-finger tap on the trackpad
The Mac menu bar adds File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Tools, Data
Settings: Excel > Preferences (Settings), not File > Options

steps.say: This is an April sales register for a furniture distributor. On the right we've written down the total, the average and the number of invoices, and we didn't type a single formula. By the end of this lesson you'll read numbers like these straight off the screen.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-01 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you'll learn the names of the parts of the Excel window, how cells and ranges are written, and what the status bar tells you. Open the practice workbook and go to the sheet called S01-01.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• The parts of the Excel window and their names
• Cells, ranges, rows and columns
• What the status bar tells you about a selection

Practice sheet: S01-01

steps.say: A workbook is the file. Each tab at the bottom is a sheet. The ribbon at the top holds the commands. The Name Box, on the left above the grid, shows where you are. The formula bar next to it shows what is really inside the cell. And the status bar at the bottom gives quick totals.

acts.t:
The Excel window
Workbook = the file   •   Sheet = one tab inside it
Ribbon = tabs of commands at the top
Name Box = the address of the selected cell
Formula bar = what is really inside the cell
Status bar = quick Sum, Average and Count of a selection

steps.say: Columns have letters and rows have numbers. Where they meet is a cell. This is cell C4: column C, row 4. Look at the Name Box. It says C4.

Now cell F4. The cell shows seventy-six thousand two hundred and fifty rupees, with a rupee sign and commas. The formula bar shows the plain number underneath. Formatting changes the look, never the value.
A group of cells is called a range. You write it as the first cell, a colon, and the last cell. A1 colon F11 is our whole table: six columns and eleven rows.
You can also select a whole column by clicking its letter. Here's column D. And a whole row by clicking its number. Here's row 4.
Now select the amounts, F2 to F11, and look at the status bar at the bottom right. Excel shows the Average, the Count and the Sum of the selection. The sum is eleven lakh rupees.
Let's write that down. Select cell I2, type eleven lakh as plain digits, one, one and five zeros, and press Return. The cell is already formatted, so it shows the rupee sign and Indian commas.
The average is one lakh ten thousand rupees, so type that in I3. The count is ten invoices, so type 10 in I4.

Here's a common slip. If you start the selection on the heading, F1 to F11, the Sum stays the same, but the Count jumps to eleven. The status bar Count counts every filled cell, text included. So start below the heading when you read a count.

One more tip. Right-click the status bar, which on a Mac means Control-click, and you can switch on Minimum, Maximum and Numerical Count. Numerical Count ignores text, so the heading would not have fooled it.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Control-click the status bar and tick:
• Minimum   • Maximum   • Numerical Count
Numerical Count counts numbers only, so headings don't sneak in.

steps.say: A few Mac differences. Control-click, or a two-finger tap on the trackpad, is the right-click. Excel for Mac also has a menu bar at the very top of the screen, and settings live under Excel, Preferences, not File, Options.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Right-click = Control-click, or a two-finger tap on the trackpad
The Mac menu bar adds File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Tools, Data
Settings: Excel > Preferences (Settings), not File > Options

steps.say: To recap. A cell is a column letter plus a row number, and a range is first cell, colon, last cell. The formula bar shows the real value. And the status bar gives you Sum, Average and Count without a formula.

acts.t:
Recap
• Cell = column letter + row number, e.g. C4
• Range = first cell : last cell, e.g. A1:F11
• Status bar = instant Sum, Average and Count of any selection

steps.say: Your challenge. Select the first five invoices only, read their sum on the status bar, and type it in I6. The answer is on the sheet S01-01 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Select the amounts of the first five invoices (F2:F6).
Read the Sum on the status bar and type it in I6.

Answer: sheet S01-01 Done

lessons.title: Moving around big sheets fast
learn: Jump to the edge of data and select to the end
Go To and the Name Box as bookmarks
lessons.mac:
Control + arrow keys often switch desktops (Mission Control). Use ⌘ + arrow in Excel.
MacBook: fn + ← = Home, fn + → = End, fn + ↑ / ↓ = Page Up / Page Down
Go To is also under Edit > Find > Go To in the menu bar

steps.say: Here's a register with six hundred transactions, a whole financial year from April to March. On the right are facts about it: the last ID, how many rows there are, and the total amount. You'll find each of them in seconds, without scrolling.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-02 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you'll jump to the edge of your data, select to the end in one move, and use Go To and the Name Box as bookmarks. The practice sheet is S01-02.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Jump to the edge of the data
• Select from here to the end in one move
• Go To, and the Name Box as a bookmark

Practice sheet: S01-02

steps.say: Four shortcuts carry this lesson. Command plus an arrow jumps to the edge of the data. Add Shift to select everything on the way. Function, Control and left arrow takes you home to A1. And Control G opens Go To.

acts.t:
Moving fast on a Mac
⌘ + arrow   jump to the last filled cell in that direction
⌘ + ⇧ + arrow   select from here to that edge
fn + ⌃ + ←   go to A1 (Control + Home)
⌃ + G   Go To a cell or a name

steps.say: We're on the practice sheet, in cell A1. Scrolling six hundred rows with a trackpad is slow, and it's easy to overshoot.
Press Command and the down arrow. Excel jumps straight to the last filled cell in column A. The last transaction is TXN 0600, in row 601.
Write it down in J2. Type TXN, dash, zero six zero zero, and press Return.
To come back to the top, press Function, Control and the left arrow. That's the MacBook version of Control Home, and it always lands on A1.
Command and the right arrow jumps across the header row to the last column, G, the amounts.

Now select every amount. Go to G2, then press Command, Shift and the down arrow. All six hundred amounts are selected. The status bar shows a Count of 600, and a Sum of three crore sixty-one lakh eighteen thousand six hundred rupees.
Type 600 in J3. Then type the total in J4, as plain digits.
Here's the catch. Start at E1, the Product column, and press Command and the down arrow. Excel stops at row 249, not at the bottom. Row 250 has a missing product, and a blank cell stops the jump.
So jump in a column with no gaps, usually the ID column. Column A has an ID in every row, so Command and down arrow from A1 always lands on the true last row.
To reach a cell you know, press Control G to open Go To. Type D350 in the Reference box and click OK. Excel takes you straight there.
You can also bookmark a range. Select I1 to J6, click in the Name Box, type the word Summary, and press Return. You've just created a named range.
Now go anywhere, say row 601. Type Summary in the Name Box, or pick it from the Name Box list, and Excel jumps back and selects the summary block.
On many Macs, Control with the arrow keys is taken by Mission Control, so use Command with the arrows in Excel. On a MacBook, Function with the arrows gives you Home, End, Page Up and Page Down.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Control + arrow keys often switch desktops (Mission Control). Use ⌘ + arrow in Excel.
MacBook: fn + ← = Home, fn + → = End, fn + ↑ / ↓ = Page Up / Page Down
Go To is also under Edit > Find > Go To in the menu bar

steps.say: To recap. Command and an arrow jumps to the edge, and adding Shift selects on the way. Blank cells stop the jump, so use a column with no gaps. And Go To and named ranges take you anywhere in one step.

acts.t:
Recap
• ⌘ + arrow jumps, ⌘ + ⇧ + arrow selects to the edge
• Blank cells stop the jump: use the ID column
• ⌃ + G and the Name Box jump to any cell or named range

steps.say: Your challenge. Find the date of the very last transaction, and the total quantity sold in column F. Type them in J5 and J6. The answers are on S01-02 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
J5: the date of the last transaction
J6: the total quantity sold (column F)
Use ⌘ + arrow and ⌘ + ⇧ + arrow, then read the status bar.

Answer: sheet S01-02 Done

lessons.title: Entering and editing data
learn: The four data types and how Excel reads them
Edit in cell, new line in a cell, fill many cells at once
lessons.mac:
Edit a cell: ⌃ + U  (F2 needs fn on most MacBooks)
New line in a cell: ⌃ + ⌥ + Return
Fill the selection: ⌘ + Return
The Mac delete key deletes backwards; fn + delete deletes forwards

steps.say: This is a vendor register from the accounts team. We'll add a new vendor, fix a typo, write a two-line remark, and mark every vendor as pending in one go. Small skills, but you'll use them every day.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-03 Done

steps.say: You'll learn the four kinds of data Excel understands, how to edit inside a cell, how to put two lines in one cell, and how to fill many cells at once. The practice sheet is S01-03.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• The four kinds of data and how Excel reads them
• Edit inside a cell, and a new line in a cell
• Fill many cells with one entry

Practice sheet: S01-03

steps.say: Excel decides what you typed the moment you press Return. Text sits on the left. Numbers sit on the right. Dates are really numbers with a date format, so they sit on the right too. TRUE and FALSE sit in the centre.

acts.t:
Four kinds of data
Text: names, codes, GSTINs  →  left aligned
Numbers: amounts, quantities  →  right aligned
Dates: numbers shown as dates  →  right aligned
TRUE / FALSE: logical values  →  centred

If a number sits on the left, Excel is treating it as text.

steps.say: Let's add a new vendor in row 7. Select A7, type the vendor code, zero zero four five seven, and press Return.
Look what happened. Excel shows 457. It read the code as a number and dropped the leading zeros. That's right for amounts, but wrong for vendor codes, PIN codes and phone numbers.
Type it again with an apostrophe in front: apostrophe, zero zero four five seven. The apostrophe tells Excel to keep it as text, and it doesn't show in the cell.
Select B7 and type the vendor name, Annapurna Caterers. Press Tab to move right. Type the city, Kolhapur, and press Tab again.
For the date, type it as year, month and day with dashes: 2026, dash, 04, dash, 15. Excel understands this order on every Mac, whatever your region setting, and the cell shows it back as 15-04-2026.
Type the amount, 35600, and press Tab. This vendor isn't GST registered, so type FALSE and press Return. Notice the alignment: text on the left, numbers and dates on the right, FALSE in the centre.
Row 4 has a typo: Navi Mumbia. Select C4 and press Control U to edit inside the cell. The cursor goes to the end of the text, so you don't have to retype the whole thing.
Press Delete twice to remove the a and the i, type a, i, and press Return. Now it reads Navi Mumbai.
Now a two-line remark. In H4, type Payment due. Then press Control, Option and Return to start a new line inside the same cell, type 30 days credit, and press Return to finish.

acts.h: Type 30 days credit and press Return

steps.say: Last, every vendor's status is Pending. Select G2 to G7, type Pending once, and press Command Return instead of plain Return. Excel puts the word into all six selected cells.
Command Return works with formulas too. Select a range, type one formula, press Command Return, and every cell gets it, with the references adjusted for each row.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Select a range → type once → ⌘ + Return
Works for text, numbers and formulas.

steps.say: On a Mac, Control U edits a cell, because F2 needs the Function key on most MacBooks. Control, Option and Return gives a new line in a cell. And the delete key on a Mac deletes backwards, like Backspace.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Edit a cell: ⌃ + U  (F2 needs fn on most MacBooks)
New line in a cell: ⌃ + ⌥ + Return
Fill the selection: ⌘ + Return
The Mac delete key deletes backwards; fn + delete deletes forwards

steps.say: To recap. Watch the alignment to see how Excel read your entry, and use an apostrophe for codes with leading zeros. Control U edits in place. And Command Return fills a whole selection at once.

acts.t:
Recap
• Left = text, right = number or date: check what Excel understood
• Apostrophe keeps leading zeros; type dates as YYYY-MM-DD
• ⌃ + U edits in place, ⌘ + Return fills a selection

steps.say: Your challenge. Add one more vendor in row 8: code 00462, Malabar Spices, Kochi, invoice date 18 April 2026, amount twenty-seven thousand four hundred rupees, GST registered TRUE, status Pending. Check it against S01-03 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge: row 8
Code 00462  •  Malabar Spices  •  Kochi
Invoice date 18-04-2026  •  Amount ₹27,400
GST Registered TRUE  •  Status Pending

Answer: sheet S01-03 Done

lessons.title: AutoFill, series and custom lists
learn: Fill dates, numbers and invoice IDs
A custom list for April-to-March months
lessons.mac:
Custom lists: Excel > Preferences (Settings) > Custom Lists
Fill Series: Home > Fill > Series
Fill handle: drag the small square at the bottom-right of the selection
Copy the cell above into a selection: ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here's an invoice log with serial numbers, invoice IDs and invoice dates on working days only, all filled in seconds. On the right, monthly sales sorted in financial-year order, April to March. That last one needs a custom list, and you'll set it up once for good.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-04 Done

steps.say: You'll fill numbers, invoice IDs and working-day dates, see why A to Z fails for months, and create an April to March custom list. Custom lists can't be made in Excel for the web, so this one is recorded in the desktop app.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Fill numbers, invoice IDs and working-day dates
• Why A to Z sorting fails for months
• A custom list for April to March

Practice sheet: S01-04
Recorded in Excel desktop (custom lists are not in Excel for the web)

steps.say: Fill Series lives on the Home tab, under Fill. Linear adds a fixed step. Date can step by day, weekday, month or year. And AutoFill copies a pattern, like an invoice ID that ends in a number.

acts.t:
Home > Fill > Series
Type: Linear (1, 2, 3…)  •  Growth (×)  •  Date  •  AutoFill (INV-2601 → INV-2602)
Date unit: Day  •  Weekday  •  Month  •  Year
Step value: how much to add each time

steps.say: The first row is filled in for you. Select A2 to A21, the serial numbers for twenty invoices.
On the Home tab, click Fill, then Series. Choose Linear, set the Step value to 1, and click OK. Excel counts from 1 to 20.
Now the invoice IDs, B2 to B21. Open Fill, Series again, and choose AutoFill. AutoFill sees the number at the end of INV 2601 and keeps counting: 2602, 2603, all the way to 2620.
For the dates, select C2 to C21 and open Series. Choose Date, and for the Date unit pick Weekday. Excel skips Saturdays and Sundays, so the twentieth invoice falls on 28 April 2026.
Now the monthly sales. They're jumbled, so let's sort them. Select E2 to F13, then choose Sort and Filter, Sort A to Z.
Here's the problem. A to Z puts April, August, December and February first. That's alphabetical, and no finance team reads months that way. We need April to March.
Excel needs to learn our order once. Click File, then Options, then Advanced.

Scroll down to the General section and click Edit Custom Lists. Column H already holds April to March, so in Import list from cells, type dollar H dollar 2, colon, dollar H dollar 13. Click Import, then OK twice.

acts.h: Set Import list from cells to $H$2:$H$13

steps.say: Select E1 to F13, this time with the headings, and on the Data tab click Sort. Tick My data has headers, sort by Month, and in the Order box choose Custom List.
Pick the April to March list, click OK, and OK again. The months now run April, May, June, through to March, the way your finance team reports them.

acts.h: Click April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December, January, February, March

steps.say: A custom list works in every workbook on this computer. It also drives AutoFill: type the first item of any custom list, drag the fill handle, and Excel fills the rest. Use it for zones, branch codes or grades.

acts.t:
Pro tip
A custom list works in every workbook on this computer.
Type the first item and drag the fill handle: Excel fills the rest of the list.
Good for zones, branch codes, grades, FY months.

steps.say: On a Mac, custom lists are under Excel, Preferences, Custom Lists. Fill Series is on the Home tab, exactly as here. And to AutoFill with the mouse, drag the small square at the corner of the selection, called the fill handle.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Custom lists: Excel > Preferences (Settings) > Custom Lists
Fill Series: Home > Fill > Series
Fill handle: drag the small square at the bottom-right of the selection
Copy the cell above into a selection: ⌘ + D

steps.say: To recap. Fill Series gives you counting numbers, patterned IDs and working-day dates. A to Z sorting is alphabetical, so months need a custom list. And you create that list once, for every workbook.

acts.t:
Recap
• Fill > Series: Linear, AutoFill for IDs, Date by Weekday
• A to Z sorts months alphabetically
• A custom list fixes the order once, for every workbook

steps.say: Your challenge. In D2, type 8 April 2026. Then fill D2 to D21 with follow-up dates every seven days, using Fill Series with Date, Day, and a Step value of 7. The answer is on S01-04 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
D2: 08-04-2026
Fill D2:D21 every 7 days: Fill > Series > Date > Day > Step value 7

Answer: sheet S01-04 Done

lessons.title: Flash Fill
learn: Split names and pull out codes by example

steps.say: Here's an employee list from HR. Full names and employee codes came in, and we needed first names, last names, a city code and an email ID for every person. All four columns were filled by example, with Flash Fill, and no formulas.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-05 Done

steps.say: You'll split names by typing one example, pull a code out of the middle of some text, and learn what to do when Flash Fill guesses wrong. The practice sheet is S01-05.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Split names by typing one example
• Pull a code out of the middle of a text
• When Flash Fill guesses wrong, and how to steer it

Practice sheet: S01-05

steps.say: Flash Fill works by example. You type the answer for the first row. Then, in the next empty cell, press Command E. Excel spots the pattern and fills the rest of the column with plain values.

acts.t:
Flash Fill   ⌘ + E
1. Type the answer for the first row yourself
2. Move to the next empty cell below
3. Press ⌘ + E: Excel copies the pattern down the column
The results are values, not formulas

steps.say: In C2, type the first name from A2, Priya, and press Return.
Now, in C3, press Command E. Excel sees that you took the first word, and fills every first name in the column, even for people with middle names.

Last names are trickier. Rahul Kumar Verma has a middle name, so a single example could teach Excel the wrong rule. Type Sharma in D2 and Verma in D3. Two examples make the rule clear: take the last word.
Select D4 and press Command E. Check the rows with middle names: Shaikh, Rathore and Gill are all correct.
Now the city code, the three letters in the middle of the employee code. Type MUM in E2. This time use the mouse: select E3, go to the Data tab, and click Flash Fill.
Every code, from DEL to CHD, is pulled out correctly. Flash Fill found the text between the two dashes.
Now a common trap. Priya's surname changes after her wedding. In A2, type Priya Menon. Look at D2. It still says Sharma. Flash Fill typed values once, and it doesn't update when the source changes.

acts.h: Type Priya Menon and press Return

steps.say: Press Command Z to undo. If your source data changes every month, use a formula instead. You'll meet TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER in the text functions section.
If Flash Fill fills nothing, check two things. The example column must touch the data, with no empty column in between. And give it one more example, from a row that looks different.

acts.t:
When Flash Fill misfires
• Keep the example column next to the data (no empty column between)
• Add a second example from an unusual row, then ⌘ + E again
• Always scan the result: Flash Fill guesses

steps.say: To recap. Type one example and press Command E. Add a second example when rows differ, like names with middle names. And remember that Flash Fill gives values that never update.

acts.t:
Recap
• Example first, then ⌘ + E (or Data > Flash Fill)
• Tricky rows? Give a second example
• Results are values: they don't update when the source changes

steps.say: Your challenge. Fill the Email ID column with first name dot last name at deccanfoods dot in, all in small letters, like priya dot sharma at deccanfoods dot in. The answers are on S01-05 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Column F: firstname.lastname@deccanfoods.in, all lowercase
e.g. priya.sharma@deccanfoods.in
Tip: give two examples, one with a middle name

Answer: sheet S01-05 Done

lessons.title: Copy, paste and Paste Special
learn: Add 10% to a whole column with Paste Special Multiply
lessons.mac:
Paste Special: ⌃ + ⌘ + V, or Edit > Paste Special in the menu bar
Quick values: Home > Paste arrow > Paste Values
Operations skip text cells

steps.say: Prices went up ten percent from 1st April. On this sheet, every base price was raised in one move, the GST prices updated themselves, and the quote column holds fixed values we can send to a client. Below, the branch targets were turned sideways. All of it with Paste Special.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-06 Done

steps.say: You'll use Paste Special to paste values, formats and transpose, raise a whole column by ten percent with Multiply, and see why a plain paste can give wrong numbers. The practice sheet is S01-06.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Paste Special: Values, Formats, Transpose
• Raise a whole column by 10% with Multiply
• Why a plain paste can give wrong numbers

Practice sheet: S01-06

steps.say: Paste Special opens with Control, Command and V. The top half chooses what to paste, such as values only or formats only. The Operation section does maths with the copied number on every selected cell.

acts.t:
Paste Special   ⌃ + ⌘ + V
Paste: All  •  Formulas  •  Values  •  Formats …
Operation: Add  •  Subtract  •  Multiply  •  Divide
Transpose: rows become columns, columns become rows

steps.say: In H2 we have 1.1. Multiplying by 1.1 adds ten percent. Select H2 and press Command C to copy it.
Select the base prices, D2 to D11, and press Control, Command and V to open Paste Special.

Under Paste, choose Values, so the prices keep their rupee format. Under Operation, choose Multiply, and click OK. Every price is ten percent higher, and the GST prices in column E updated by themselves.
Now the quote column. We want the GST prices as fixed numbers. The obvious move is to copy E2 to E11 with Command C, select F2, and press Command V.
Look at F2. Thirteen thousand and nineteen rupees, not eleven thousand and thirty-three. A plain paste copied the formula, and the formula moved one column right, so it's adding GST on top of GST.

Press Command Z to undo. E2 to E11 is still copied, so select F2, open Paste Special, choose Values and click OK. F2 now shows eleven thousand and thirty-three rupees, as a plain number that won't change.

Next, formats. The branch table at the bottom has a plain heading. Copy A1, select A14 to B14, open Paste Special, choose Formats and click OK. Only the look is copied: the dark fill and white bold text.
Finally, transpose. Copy A14 to B18, select D14, open Paste Special, tick Transpose and click OK. The four branches now run across a row, ready for a dashboard.

On a Mac, Paste Special is also in the menu bar under Edit. For a quick paste of values, use the arrow under the Paste button on the Home tab. And Multiply only touches numbers; text cells are left alone.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Paste Special: ⌃ + ⌘ + V, or Edit > Paste Special in the menu bar
Quick values: Home > Paste arrow > Paste Values
Operations skip text cells

steps.say: To recap. Paste Values freezes results so formulas can't drift. Paste Special Multiply changes a whole column in one move. And Formats and Transpose copy the look, or turn a list sideways.

acts.t:
Recap
• Plain paste moves formulas: use Values to freeze results
• Operation Multiply: a whole column +10% in one go
• Formats copies the look; Transpose turns rows into columns

steps.say: Your challenge. Copy the item names in B2 to B11 and transpose them into row 21, starting at A21. The answer is on S01-06 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Transpose the item names B2:B11 into row 21, starting at A21.

Answer: sheet S01-06 Done

lessons.title: Rows, columns and sheets
learn: Insert, delete, hide, move and resize
Rename, colour, copy and group sheets
lessons.mac:
Rename: double-click the sheet tab
Control-click a tab: Insert, Delete, Rename, Move or Copy, Tab Color
Group: Shift-click (a run) or ⌘-click (one by one)
Insert rows/columns also via the menu bar: Insert > Rows / Columns

steps.say: Here's an employee list after a quick tidy-up. A duplicate row is gone, there's a new Designation column, City sits next to it, and the salary column is hidden before the sheet is shared. We'll also rename, colour, group and copy sheets.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-07 Done

steps.say: You'll insert, delete, move, resize and hide rows and columns, then rename, colour, group and copy sheets. Grouping sheets isn't available in Excel for the web, so this lesson is recorded in the desktop app.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Insert, delete, move, resize and hide rows and columns
• Rename, colour, group and copy sheets

Practice sheet: S01-07 (plus the Pune and Nagpur sheets)
Recorded in Excel desktop (grouping sheets is not in Excel for the web)

steps.say: Rows 5 and 6 are the same person, Prakash Hegde, entered twice. Let's remove row 6.
Many people select the cells and press the Delete key. That only clears the contents. The empty row stays, leaving a gap in the middle of the list.
Undo with Command Z. Select the whole of row 6 by its number, then on the Home tab click the Delete arrow and choose Delete Sheet Rows. The rows below move up, with no gap.
We need a Designation column after Name. Select column C, then choose Home, Insert, Insert Sheet Columns. A blank column appears and everything shifts right. In C1, type Designation.

Now move City next to Designation. Select column E, City, and cut it with Command X. Select column D, right-click, which is Control-click on a Mac, and choose Insert Cut Cells. City moves in and Department shifts right.
Designation needs room. Select column C and choose Home, Format, Column Width. Type 20 and click OK. You can also double-click the line between two column letters to fit the contents.

Salaries shouldn't travel with this sheet. Select column G, Monthly CTC, and choose Home, Format, Hide and Unhide, Hide Columns. The column letters now jump from F to H. That's how you spot a hidden column.
Now sheets. Go to the Pune sheet and choose Home, Format, Rename Sheet. Type Pune Apr and press Return. Double-clicking the tab does the same thing.

acts.h: Type Pune Apr and press Return

steps.say: In the same menu, choose Tab Color and pick Green. Colour-coded tabs help when a workbook has twenty sheets.
To change two sheets at once, group them. Hold Shift and click the Nagpur tab. Both tabs are selected and the title bar says Group. Type a title in A1, and it goes on both sheets.

acts.h: Type Attendance - April 2026 and press Return

steps.say: Always ungroup straight after. Click any sheet outside the group, and the Group label disappears. Typing into grouped sheets by accident is a classic way to overwrite data.
To copy a sheet, for example to start May, go to Pune Apr and choose Home, Format, Move or Copy Sheet. Pick move to end, tick Create a copy, and click OK. You get Pune Apr two, ready to rename.

acts.h: Go to the sheet Pune Apr
Set Before sheet to (move to end)

steps.say: On a Mac, double-click a tab to rename it, and Control-click a tab for Insert, Delete, Tab Color and Move or Copy. Shift-click tabs to group a run of sheets, or Command-click to pick them one by one.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Rename: double-click the sheet tab
Control-click a tab: Insert, Delete, Rename, Move or Copy, Tab Color
Group: Shift-click (a run) or ⌘-click (one by one)
Insert rows/columns also via the menu bar: Insert > Rows / Columns

steps.say: To recap. Delete Sheet Rows removes a row, while the Delete key only clears it. Insert Cut Cells moves a column without overwriting anything. And always ungroup sheets as soon as you're done.

acts.t:
Recap
• Delete key clears; Delete Sheet Rows removes
• Cut + Insert Cut Cells moves a column safely
• Hidden columns show as a jump in the letters; ungroup sheets right after use

lessons.title: Find and Replace
lessons.mac:
Find: ⌘ + F   •   Replace: ⌃ + H
Menu bar: Edit > Find > Replace
Wildcards and match options work the same

steps.say: This order list came from three different people. Bengaluru was spelt two ways, Private Limited was written three ways, and Maharashtra was sometimes just MH. Here it is, cleaned up with Find and Replace, including a second sheet of returns.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-08 Done

steps.say: You'll replace text across the whole workbook, use wildcards to catch spelling variations, and use Match entire cell contents so you don't change too much. The practice sheet is S01-08.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Replace across the whole workbook
• Wildcards: * and ?
• Match entire cell contents

Practice sheet: S01-08

steps.say: Replace is on the Home tab, under Find and Select. A star means any number of characters, and a question mark means exactly one. Match entire cell contents changes only cells that are exactly your text.

acts.t:
Home > Find & Select > Replace   (⌃ + H)
Find what  →  Replace with
* = any number of characters   ? = exactly one
Match entire cell contents: only cells that are exactly this text
Within: Sheet or Workbook

steps.say: On the practice sheet, open the Home tab, click Find and Select, then Replace.
In Find what, type Bangalore. In Replace with, type Bengaluru. Set Within to Workbook, so the Returns sheet is fixed too, and click Replace All.
Close the dialog and check the Returns sheet. Both Bangalore entries there say Bengaluru as well.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-08 Returns

steps.say: Now the company names: Pvt dot Ltd dot, Pvt Ltd, and Pvt Ltd with a full stop. Open Replace again. In Find what, type Pvt, star, Ltd, star. Replace with Pvt Ltd, set Within back to Sheet, and click Replace All.
Close the dialog. Every company name now ends the same way, which matters later when you count orders per customer.
Next, MH in the State column. Open Replace, find MH, replace with Maharashtra, and click Replace All.
But look at B4. MHK Steels has become MaharashtraK Steels. Replace changed MH wherever it appeared, even inside a company name.
Undo with Command Z. Open Replace again and this time tick Match entire cell contents, so only cells that are exactly MH change. Click Replace All. MHK Steels is safe.
Before a big replace, click Find All first. Excel lists every matching cell, so you can see what will change. And to find a real star or question mark, put a tilde in front of it.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Click Find All before Replace All to preview every match.
Searching for a real * or ?  Type ~* or ~?

steps.say: On a Mac, Command F opens Find, and Control H opens Replace. Both are also in the menu bar, under Edit, Find.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Find: ⌘ + F   •   Replace: ⌃ + H
Menu bar: Edit > Find > Replace
Wildcards and match options work the same

steps.say: To recap. Within Workbook fixes every sheet at once. A star catches spelling variations. And Match entire cell contents stops a replace from changing text inside longer words.

acts.t:
Recap
• Within: Workbook to fix every sheet
• * and ? catch variations
• Match entire cell contents prevents over-replacing

lessons.title: Challenge 1: build a staff contact list
learn: Use everything from this section on a raw list

steps.say: Time to put this section together. HR has sent a raw staff list: full names, employee codes, the old city name Bombay in places, and salaries in thousands. Your job is to turn it into a clean contact list.
The six tasks are on the right, from column J: serial numbers, first and last names, city codes, a city clean-up, salaries in rupees, and a total from the status bar.
Pause the video now and try all six tasks on sheet S01-09. When you're done, press play to watch the solution.

acts.t:
Your turn
Pause now and complete the six tasks on sheet S01-09.
Press play when you're done to see the solution.

Answers: sheet S01-09 Answers

steps.say: Here's the solution. Task one. In A2, type 1. In A3, type equals A2 plus 1. Then select A3 to A16 and press Command D to fill down. Each row adds one to the row above, so you get 1 to 15.

acts.h: Select A3:A16 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Task two. In F2, type Aarti and press Return. Then select F3 and press Command E. Flash Fill takes the first word of every name.
For last names, type Deshmukh in G2, and give a second example from a name with a middle name: Iyer in G3. Select G4 and press Command E.
Task three. Type PUN in H2, select H3, and press Command E for every city code.
Task four. Open Replace, find Bombay, replace with Mumbai, tick Match entire cell contents, and click Replace All. Three cells change.
Task five. Type 1000 in J13 and copy it. Select E2 to E16, open Paste Special with Control, Command and V, choose Values and Multiply, and click OK. Sixty-eight becomes sixty-eight thousand rupees.
Then rename the heading. In E1, type Monthly CTC, rupees in brackets.

acts.h: Type Monthly CTC (₹) and press Return

steps.say: Task six. Select E2 to E16. The status bar shows a sum of ten lakh thirty-three thousand rupees. Type it in E17.
Compare your sheet with S01-09 Answers. If everything matches, you've used every skill from section one.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S01-09 Answers

steps.say: Well done. You filled a series, split text with Flash Fill, cleaned data with Replace, converted a column with Paste Special, and read a total from the status bar. Next, we'll make sheets like this look professional.

acts.t:
Section 1 skills used
• Fill down and Flash Fill
• Replace with Match entire cell contents
• Paste Special Multiply
• Status bar totals
